This review summarizes current evidence, spanning expression associations, regulator-dependent phenotypes and site-specific m6A mechanisms, linking METTL3, METTL14, FTO, ALKBH5, YTHDF proteins and IGF2BP family members to AML biology and therapy resistance. We focus on chemotherapy, venetoclax, anthracycline and differentiation-therapy resistance, and on preclinical and early clinical agents targeting METTL3, FTO, ALKBH5 and selected readers. We also discuss limitations in current evidence, including context-dependent transcript regulation, incomplete distinction between catalytic m6A-dependent and non-catalytic regulator functions, correlative immune and pediatric prognostic associations, uncertain therapeutic windows, biomarker heterogeneity and challenges in measuring functionally relevant m6A changes in patient samples. These issues should be addressed before m6A-directed strategies can be incorporated into AML precision therapy.

articles.title: Global epidemiology and genetic evolution of enterovirus D68 over a decade (2015-24): a systematic review.
articles.abstract: Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a persistent global health concern, causing mild to severe respiratory disease and, in rare cases, acute flaccid myelitis, a polio-like paralytic syndrome. In this systematic review, we synthesised global data on the epidemiology and genetic evolution of EV-D68 from 2015 to 2024 and show its continued widespread circulation and concerning severity. 8184 EV-D68 cases were reported by 44 countries, and 267 (3·3%) of these cases were EV-D68-associated acute flaccid paralysis cases reported by 26 countries, across all continents. Biennial upsurges followed a distinct every-even-year pattern until 2020, after which the circulation showed geographical diversification in Europe and North America, possibly influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic. EV-D68 remained associated with severe respiratory disease and acute flaccid myelitis, not only primarily in children younger than five years but also increasingly in adults. Individuals who progressed to acute flaccid paralysis had poor prognosis for full recovery. Genotypic shifts were marked by the dominance of subgenotype B3 since 2016 and A2/D since 2018, with novel variants emerging for both after 2020. Despite limitations in surveillance quality and coverage, the findings underscore the need for sustained surveillance, improved diagnostic strategies, and targeted interventions to mitigate EV-D68-related morbidity.

articles.title: Interventions for managing immature permanent teeth with necrotic pulps.
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Immature permanent teeth with necrotic pulps are difficult candidates for conventional root canal fillings. Interventions for management of such teeth include regenerative endodontic procedures (REPs), apexification, and root strengthening interventions. Basic principles involve removal of necrotic pulp, canal debridement and infection control. Currently, there is no evidence-based guidance to manage such teeth.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the effects of different interventions to manage immature permanent teeth with necrotic pulps.
SEARCH METHODS: We used CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Oral Health specialised register, and two trials registers, together with reference checking, to identify studies that were included in the review. The latest search date was October 2025.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing additions to autologous blood clot (BC) scaffolds in REPs with conventional BC scaffolds in REPs for managing necrotic pulps in immature permanent teeth in children. We also included RCTs comparing different additions to BC scaffolds, coronal sealing materials, and intracanal disinfectants in REPs, different approaches to apexification, REPS (using any approach) with apexification, and root strengthening interventions.
OUTCOMES: Our outcomes were clinical measures of success (measured as absence of pain, or clinical success as defined by study authors), root apex development (prioritising measures of apical closure), discolouration, endodontic complications, patient-reported quality of life, and periodontal health. We prioritised data reported at 12 months, but collected data at later time points.
RISK OF BIAS: We used the Cochrane RoB 1 tool to assess bias in the RCTs.
SYNTHESIS METHODS: Although we planned to synthesise results for each outcome using meta-analysis, pooling was not possible owing to the sparse data for each outcome. Given the large number of comparisons in this review, we prioritised reporting data for scaffolds in REPs - in particular, additions to BC scaffolds compared with conventional BC scaffolds - because we believed that these were the most clinically relevant comparisons. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome in this main comparison.
INCLUDED STUDIES: Overall, we included 30 RCTs in which 1227 teeth in 1152 children were treated. Studies included 37 different comparisons of REP interventions (scaffolds, coronal sealing materials, intracanal disinfectants), apexification approaches, and REPs versus apexification. No studies assessed root strengthening interventions.
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: For our main comparison, we included eight studies (351 treated teeth) comparing platelet concentrate or synthetic additions to BC scaffolds with conventional BC scaffolds. We judged the certainty of the evidence for the following outcomes to be very low owing to risks of bias and high levels of imprecision. Therefore, we had very little confidence in the effect estimates. Platelet-rich plasma (1 study, 31 teeth). At 12 months, the evidence is very uncertain whether there are any differences between scaffold types in clinical success (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.28), or discolouration (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.36). Platelet-rich fibrin (1 study, 38 or 22 teeth). The evidence is very uncertain whether there are any differences between scaffold types in clinical success at 24 months (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.15), the number of teeth with calcific bridge at the apical level at 12 months (RR 1.40, 95% CI 0.64 to 3.07), or discolouration at 12 months (presence of discolouration reported in all teeth). Platelet pellet (1 study, 38 teeth). At 24 months, the evidence is very uncertain whether there are any differences between scaffold types in clinical success (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.20). Advanced platelet-rich fibrin (1 study, 18 teeth). The study included in this comparison reported no relevant review outcome measures. Concentrated growth factor (1 study, 54 teeth). At 12 months, the evidence is very uncertain whether there are any differences between scaffold types in clinical success (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.16), or periodontal health (resolution of periapical radiolucency: RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.84 to 2.53). Synthetic collagen-based addition (1 study, 43 teeth). At 18 months, the evidence is very uncertain whether there are any differences between scaffold types in discolouration (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.70), or endodontic complications: the number of teeth with pulp calcifications: RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.57). Growth factors-impregnated synthetic addition (1 study, 17 teeth). The study included in this comparison reported no relevant review outcome measures.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: We could not draw conclusions regarding the effectiveness of different additions to BC scaffolds compared with conventional BC scaffolds used in REPs owing to very low-certainty evidence in reported outcome measures, or absence of evidence for many critical outcomes (and absence of any evidence for some comparisons). We did not formally assess the certainty of the evidence for comparisons of other interventions in the review, but note that the evidence included similarly small studies with high or unclear risks of bias. No studies reported pain or patient-reported quality of life, and further research emphasising patient-reported outcomes may provide evidence for practice. Whilst studies often reported other measures, particularly for root apex development (such as increase in root length, or root canal wall thickness), these are less clinically informative. The absence of evidence using informative clinical measures in this review highlights the need for a core outcome set in this research field.
FUNDING: This Cochrane review was funded (in part) by University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine.
REGISTRATION: Protocol available via https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD012709.

articles.title: Curcuma longa (turmeric) or its active ingredients for osteoarthritis.
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Osteoarthritis is a major cause of disability worldwide. Current treatments have limited efficacy. Curcuma longa (turmeric) contains curcuminoids with anti-inflammatory properties that may modulate osteoarthritis pathophysiology. However, the clinical benefits and safety of Curcuma longa in osteoarthritis remain uncertain.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and harms of Curcuma longa extracts or сurcuminoids for osteoarthritis.
SEARCH METHODS: We used CENTRAL, MEDLINE, five other databases, and two trials registers, together with reference checking, to identify the studies included in the review. The latest search date was 7 November 2025. We applied no restrictions on language, publication date, or publication status.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing Curcuma longa extracts or curcuminoids to placebo, in people with osteoarthritis in any joint. Other comparators included no treatment, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), non-NSAID analgesics, or other active comparators. We focused on oral formulations of Curcuma longa, with or without bioavailability enhancers, and excluded combination products containing other active herbal compounds.
OUTCOMES: Critical outcomes included pain, function, quality of life, participant-reported global assessment of success, adverse events, withdrawals due to adverse events, and serious adverse events. The primary time point was up to three months.
RISK OF BIAS: We used Cochrane's RoB 2 tool to assess bias in the RCTs.
SYNTHESIS METHODS: We used a random-effects model for meta-analysis. We assessed the trustworthiness of all trials eligible for inclusion using the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Trustworthiness Screening Tool.
INCLUDED STUDIES: We included nine RCTs involving 1245 participants with knee osteoarthritis. The mean age of participants ranged from 52 years to 62 years; 67% of participants were female. All trials were short (up to 90 days) and investigated different Curcuma longa formulations. One trial evaluated a bioavailability-enhanced Curcuma longa formulation, while others did not report the use of bio-enhancers. Two trials used Curcuma longa extract with essential oils. Four trials used standardised or rhizome extracts of Curcuma longa, with curcuminoid content varying from 23% to 88%. Four trials compared Curcuma longa with placebo (379 participants), four with NSAIDs (673 participants), and one with paracetamol (193 participants). Here, we limit reporting to the primary comparison, Curcuma longa versus placebo. We judged three (75%) placebo-controlled trials to be at low risk of bias for pain, function, and quality of life outcomes. Two trials (50%) were at low risk of bias for safety outcomes.
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Low-certainty evidence downgraded for indirectness and publication bias showed that, compared with placebo, Curcuma longa may result in little to no difference in pain, function, or quality of life, and may improve participant-reported global assessment of success. We are very uncertain about the effect of Curcuma longa on adverse events, withdrawals due to adverse events, and serious adverse events due to very low-certainty evidence, downgraded for publication bias, imprecision, and indirectness. By three months, the mean change in pain (0 to 10 scale, 0 = no pain) was -1.57 points with placebo and 0.72 points lower (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.39 points lower to 0.06 points lower) with Curcuma longa (I² = 0%; 4 studies, 349 participants). The effect did not reach clinical significance of 1.5 points. By three months, the mean change in function (0 to 100, 0 = best function) was -5.42 points with placebo and 3.5 points lower with Curcuma longa (95% CI 7.29 points lower to 0.29 points higher; I² = 0%; 4 studies, 348 participants). By three months, the mean change in quality of life (0 to 100 scale, 100 = best quality of life) was 9.83 points with placebo and 2.19 points higher (95% CI 1.56 points lower to 5.94 points higher) with Curcuma longa (I² = 0%; 3 studies, 291 participants). By three months, 107 of 1000 participants receiving placebo reported treatment success, compared with 191 of 1000 receiving Curcuma longa (risk ratio (RR) 1.78, 95% CI 1.19 to 2.67; 2 studies, 170 participants). At the end of follow-up, 224 of 1000 participants in the placebo group reported adverse events compared with 226 of 1000 in the Curcuma longa group (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.51; I² = 0%; 4 studies, 379 participants). At the end of follow-up, 46 of 1000 participants in the placebo group withdrew due to adverse events compared with 66 of 1000 in the Curcuma longa group (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.61 to 3.43; I² = 0%; 3 studies, 321 participants). Three trials reported no serious adverse events, while one trial reported two serious adverse events in the placebo group that were unrelated to the study.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Compared with placebo, Curcuma longa may result in little to no improvement in pain, function, or quality of life, and may improve participant-reported global assessment of success in people with knee osteoarthritis. We are very uncertain about the effect of Curcuma longa on adverse events, withdrawals due to adverse events, and serious adverse events. Future studies should last longer than three months; the maximum duration of the included studies was three months. The current evidence is limited to knee osteoarthritis, and future studies should include people with hand and hip osteoarthritis.
FUNDING: No external funding was received for this work.
REGISTRATION: Protocol (2021): 10.1002/14651858.CD014683.

articles.title: Medical adhesive-related skin injuries and medical device-related pressure injuries in newborns: a scoping review.
articles.abstract: This is a protocol for a Cochrane review (flexible). The objectives are as follows: To map information on the incidence, characteristics, risk factors, and preventive strategies for MDRPI and MARSI in newborns. Based on the findings, we hope to identify knowledge gaps and to guide future research, improve treatments, and reduce injuries.

articles.title: Daily iron supplementation for prevention or treatment of iron-deficiency anaemia in infants, children, and adolescents.
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Globally, 604.8 million women and 269 million children are living with anaemia; reducing anaemia is a key goal of the 2030 Global Strategy for Women's, Children's, and Adolescents' Health.
OBJECTIVES: To determine the benefits and harms of daily oral iron supplementation in infants, children and adolescents 0-19 years of age with or without anaemia caused by iron deficiency (IDA).
SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, CINAHL, 16 additional databases, and two trial registries up to January 2025.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included 0-19-year-olds regardless of baseline iron or anaemia status. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs assessing the effects of daily oral supplementation of iron alone, iron with folic acid (IFA), or iron with other vitamins or minerals or both (iron + vitamins/minerals) versus no intervention/placebo.
OUTCOMES: Critical outcomes were anaemia, ID, IDA, growth, morbidity (respiratory illness, cough/difficulty breathing, diarrhoea, fever), and adverse events (AE) (vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation, and stool discolouration).
RISK OF BIAS: We used the Risk of bias (RoB) 1 tool.
SYNTHESIS METHODS: We used random-effects for meta-analysis and GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence.
INCLUDED STUDIES: We meta-analysed 101 studies (50,325 participants) and narratively described 13 additional studies.
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Daily oral supplementation with iron alone versus no intervention/placebo Iron supplementation versus no intervention/placebo makes little to no difference to height/length-for-age z-score ((H(L)AZ), MD -0.01, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.02; 17 studies, 5534 participants; high-certainty evidence); weight-for-height/length z-score ((W(H(L)Z), MD 0.06, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.14; 10 studies, 2683 participants; high-certainty evidence); cough (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.11; 4 studies, 2259 participants; high-certainty evidence), fever (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.02; 5 studies, 763 participants; high-certainty evidence), and respiratory illness (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.18; 3 studies, 549 participants; high-certainty evidence), but probably decreases IDA (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.30; 13 studies, 3193 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Iron supplementation may result in little to no difference in vomiting (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.43; 5 studies, 2208 participants; low-certainty evidence) and diarrhoea (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.92; 5 studies, 2018 participants; low-certainty evidence), but evidence is very uncertain for constipation (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.66; 6 studies, 1002 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Evidence is very uncertain, but supplementation may decrease anaemia (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.63; 19 studies, 5093 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and ID (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.57; 13 studies, 3977 participants; very low-certainty evidence), but may increase stool discolouration (RR 6.13, 95% CI 3.30 to 11.38; 3 studies, 315 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Daily supplementations of IFA versus folic acid (FA) alone No data were found. Daily oral supplementation of IFA versus no intervention/placebo IFA versus no intervention/placebo probably decreases ID (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.39; 1 study, 225 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and IDA (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.37; 1 study, 225 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), but evidence is very uncertain about the effects on anaemia (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.24 to 1.16; 5 studies, 1757 participants; very low-certainty evidence). IFA makes little to no difference to morbidity (diarrhoea: RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.15; 2 studies, 12,981 participants; high-certainty evidence; or respiratory illness: RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.21; 1 study, 12,679 participants; high-certainty evidence). Daily oral supplementation of iron with vitamins/minerals versus the supplementation of the same vitamins/minerals without iron Supplementation of iron with vitamins/minerals makes little to no difference to H(L)AZ (MD -0.08, 95% CI -0.17 to -0.00; 7 studies, 1638 participants; high-certainty evidence), WH(L)Z (MD 0.00, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.10; 6 studies, 1376 participants; high-certainty evidence), and diarrhoea (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.02; 4 studies, 1038 participants; high-certainty evidence). Iron supplementation probably decreases IDA (RR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.38; 4 studies, 559 participants; moderate-certainty evidence); probably makes little to no difference to cough (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.20; 2 studies, 430 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and respiratory illness (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.27; 2 studies, 430 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), and probably increases vomiting (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.02; 1 study, 243 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Evidence is very uncertain, but iron supplementation may decrease anaemia (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.87; 9 studies, 1772 participants; very low-certainty evidence); however, the effects on ID (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.05 to 1.79; 5 studies, 923 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and fever (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.03; 2 studies, 430 participants; very low-certainty evidence) are very uncertain. Daily oral supplementation of iron with vitamins/minerals versus no intervention/placebo Supplementation of iron with vitamins/minerals versus no intervention/placebo increases H(L)AZ (MD 0.08, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.11; 10 studies, 1525 participants; high-certainty evidence) and probably decreases ID (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.55; 9 studies, 1254 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Iron supplementation may increase vomiting (RR 1.96, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.96; 1 study, 162 participants; low-certainty evidence; 0-5 month-old infants) but may decrease IDA (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.83; 6 studies, 912 participants; low-certainty evidence), and may reduce anaemia, but the evidence is very uncertain (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.83; 13 studies, 2254 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Evidence is very uncertain about the effects on cough (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.25; 2 studies, 387 participants; very low-certainty evidence), fever (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.53; 2 studies, 290 participants; very low-certainty evidence), respiratory illness (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.34; 4 studies, 14,061 participants; very low-certainty evidence), and diarrhoeal morbidity (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.23 to 2.21; 3 studies, 13,861 participants; very low-certainty evidence).
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Daily oral supplementation of iron alone, iron with FA, or iron with vitamins/minerals may result in a significant reduction of iron-deficiency anaemia across our target population with little to no difference in morbidity, and a probable increase in stool discolouration.
FUNDING: Cornell Joan Klein Jacobs Center for Precision Nutrition and Health, Cornell University, (USA); World Health Organization (Switzerland) REGISTRATION: Protocol (2018) DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD013227.

articles.title: Kangaroo mother care to reduce morbidity and mortality in low birthweight infants.
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Kangaroo mother care (KMC) comprises three core components: prolonged skin-to-skin contact between infants and caregivers; support for exclusive breastfeeding; and early discharge with appropriate follow-up. It provides thermal regulation and stabilizes cardiorespiratory and feeding functions. For low birthweight infants, KMC provides a feasible, low-cost approach to care that promotes thermal regulation, stabilizes cardiorespiratory and feeding functions, and minimizes parent-infant separation. This review updates a Cochrane review first published in 2003, with subsequent updates in 2011, 2014, and 2016.
OBJECTIVES: To determine the benefits and harms of kangaroo mother care (KMC) in low birthweight infants as an alternative to conventional neonatal care before or after the initial period of stabilization with conventional care.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, CINAHL and trials registries in August 2025. We checked reference lists of included studies, and systematic reviews where subject matter related to the intervention or population examined in this review.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) where participants were hospitalized preterm infants (defined as < 37 weeks' gestation) or low birthweight infants (defined as birthweight < 2500 g). We included studies that evaluated KMC, defined as skin-to-skin contact between caregiver and infant, regardless of duration ('any KMC'), as well as KMC meeting the World Health Organization (WHO) definition (minimum duration of eight hours per day). Eligible comparisons were: any KMC compared with conventional neonatal care (CNC).
OUTCOMES: Critical outcomes were: in-hospital mortality or before 40 to 41 weeks' postmenstrual age (PMA); weight (g) at discharge or at 40 to 41 weeks' PMA; exclusive breastfeeding at discharge or at 40 to 41 weeks' PMA; any breastfeeding at discharge or at 40 to 41 weeks' PMA; length of hospital stay; nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infection or sepsis (as defined in individual studies) at any time point, and hypothermia (as defined in individual studies) at any time point.
RISK OF BIAS: We used the Cochrane Risk of bias tool 2.0 (RoB 2).
SYNTHESIS METHODS: We conducted meta-analyses using fixed-effect models to calculate risk ratios (RR) and risk difference (RD) for dichotomous data, and mean differences (MDs) for continuous data, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We evaluated the certainty of evidence using GRADE.
INCLUDED STUDIES: We included 49 RCTs enrolling 7724 infants. Studies were published between 1988 and 2024. All studies compared any KMC with CNC; 13 delivered WHO-defined KMC for 8 to 24 hours/day, while the remainder offered KMC for different durations. Thus, the 'any KMC' comparison encompasses a range of exposure durations, not solely the WHO-defined intervention. Twenty-two studies were conducted in low- or middle-income countries. We identified eight ongoing studies.
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: Any KMC likely reduces in-hospital mortality or before 40 to 41 weeks' PMA (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.99; I² = 0%; 14 studies, 4389 participants; moderate-certainty evidence; RD -0.01, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.00, I2 = 0%) and nosocomial infection or sepsis (as defined in individual studies) (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.82; I² = 45%; 15 studies, 3852 participants; moderate-certainty evidence; RD -0.03, 95% CI -0.05 to -0.02, I2 = 75%) compared to CNC. KMC may increase exclusive breastfeeding (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.27; I² = 58%; 9 studies, 1846 participants; low-certainty evidence; RD 0.10, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.14, I2 = 73%) and reduce hypothermia (as defined in individual studies) at any time point (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.86; I² = 87%; 13 studies, 3493 participants; low-certainty evidence; RD -0.11, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.09, I2 = 93%). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of any KMC on weight (g) at discharge or at 40 to 41 weeks' PMA (MD 63.00, 95% CI 40.57 to 85.43; I² = 80%; 7 studies, 1648 participants; very low-certainty evidence), any breastfeeding at discharge or at 40 to 41 weeks' PMA (RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.21; I² = 68%; 6 studies, 1282 participants; very low-certainty evidence), and length of hospital stay (days) (MD 1.19, 95% CI 1.18 to 1.21; I² = 98%; 14 studies, 3765 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Subgroup analyses suggested differences in some outcomes by KMC definition and country income, but these findings require cautious interpretation. Certainty of the evidence varies from moderate for mortality and nosocomial infection or sepsis, low for exclusive breastfeeding and hypothermia, and very low for weight, any breastfeeding and length of hospital stay. Downgrading reflected risk of bias (unclear allocation concealment, unblinded outcome assessment, maternal-reported breastfeeding outcomes), inconsistency from heterogeneity and variable outcome definitions, indirectness from heterogeneous KMC delivery, and imprecision.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: KMC probably provides clinically important benefits compared with CNC, particularly by reducing mortality and nosocomial infection or sepsis. It may also improve breastfeeding outcomes and reduce hypothermia. Effects on growth and duration of hospitalization remain very uncertain because of substantial heterogeneity and very low-certainty evidence. Evidence for mortality and infection came predominantly from low- and lower-middle-income countries, with limited and imprecise evidence from high-income settings, restricting conclusions about applicability across settings. These conclusions apply to a broad definition of KMC; only a minority of trials evaluated KMC that met the WHO duration criterion, so the pooled results should not be taken as specific estimates of WHO-defined KMC. Future research should prioritize how KMC can be delivered effectively across health systems, income settings, and infant populations, including contemporary high-income neonatal care settings. Studies should clearly describe intervention components, including whether KMC meets the WHO definition, timing of initiation, daily duration, continuity, setting, provider, and implementation fidelity. Adequately powered trials and implementation studies should use standardized outcome definitions and address outcomes for which evidence remains very uncertain, including growth, hypothermia, and duration of hospitalization. Longer-term follow-up should assess mortality, neurodevelopment, breastfeeding, growth, family-centred outcomes, adverse effects, resource use, cost-effectiveness, equity, and feasibility.
FUNDING: None.
REGISTRATION: Original review (2003): doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002771 Last review update (2016): doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD002771.pub4.

articles.title: Deer velvet antler peptides protect premature ovarian insufficiency by modulating CHK2-TAp63α signaling and gut microbiota.
articles.abstract: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is a prevalent complication among childhood, adolescent, and young adult (CAYA) cancer survivors, yet lacks effective treatments. Here we show that therapeutic gavage of deer velvet antler peptides (DVAP) reversed the reduction of primordial follicles (PFs), enhanced fertility, and suppressed apoptosis in cyclophosphamide (CTX)-induced POI mice by modulating the gut microbiota and the CHK2-TAp63α signaling pathway. Prophylactic DVAP treatment similarly mitigated PF loss. Crucially, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from DVAP-treated POI mice recapitulated the protective effects, while antibiotic-mediated gut microbiota depletion abolished DVAP's therapeutic benefits, confirming gut microbiota as the primary mediator. Notably, DVAP reshaped the gut microbial composition by enriching Lactobacillus and Limosilactobacillus genera, both positively correlated with PF preservation. Furthermore, several phosphatidylinositol (PI) species in feces, including PI(18:0/PGF1α), PI(PGF1α/20:1(11Z)), and PI(PGF1α/20:2(11Z,14Z)) exhibited correlations with these enriched bacterial taxa. These results identify DVAP as a potential fertoprotective agent against POI via the gut-ovary axis.

articles.title: Mucosal vaccination with hemagglutinin stalk provides broad protection against influenza virus subtypes in mice.
articles.abstract: Influenza viruses continually evolve through antigenic drift and shift, spreading via respiratory droplets and aerosols. Developing a universal nasal vaccine is essential for preventing seasonal and pandemic infections by inducing long-lasting immunity in the respiratory tract. The neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) transfers IgG Abs across the epithelial barrier. This study investigates whether the i.n. delivery of the conserved Stalk antigen of HA, utilizing the FcRn, can stimulate protective immune responses against various influenza virus subtypes. We engineered a monomeric IgG Fc fused to a modified HA Stalk in its prefusion form. Mice i.n. immunized with Stalk-Fc exhibited significant protection against infections from H1N1, H5N1, H6N2, and H9N2 compared with groups of control mice. The immunized mice produced long-lasting HA Stalk-specific IgA and IgG Abs in nasal washes, bronchoalveolar lavage, and blood, along with tissue-resident memory T cells in the lungs and long-lived plasma cells in the bone marrow. This led to notably lower viral replication in the nasal turbinate and lungs. The Stalk-specific Abs demonstrated strong cross-reactivity against different influenza subtypes through neutralization, Ab- or complement-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, or phagocytosis. These results indicate that FcRn efficiently transports HA Stalk-Fc across the respiratory epithelial barrier, supporting the development of a universal influenza nasal vaccine.

articles.title: The changing burden of disease in Türkiye, 1990-2023: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Türkiye has had improvements in population health over the past three decades, driven by the Health Transformation Programme launched in 2003, which expanded primary care through the family medicine system and, through the General Health Insurance Scheme, extended population coverage to near-universal levels. However, recent shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the catastrophic February 2023 earthquakes, have caused temporary reverses in health gains.
METHODS: We used Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023 estimates for Türkiye, produced using the standard GBD methods applied to all 204 countries and territories, to describe age-standardised trends from 1990 to 2023 in life expectancy, healthy life expectancy (HALE), mortality, years of life lost, years lived with disability, disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), and risk-attributable burden, by sex, age, and cause. Estimates are reported as means of 250 draws with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs). The effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and of the February 2023 earthquakes are described by examining the annual series across 2019-23 and, for the earthquakes, the burden assigned to the GBD cause exposure to forces of nature in 2023.
FINDINGS: Between 1990 and 2023, Türkiye's life expectancy increased from 68·1 years to 76·1 years (male: 65·2 years to 73·9 years; female: 71·2 years to 78·3 years), and HALE from 58·7 years to 65·1 years. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a 2·0-year decline in life expectancy, whereas the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes resulted in over 53 000 deaths. Age-standardised all-cause mortality declined by 34·9% from 1040·3 (95% UI 1022·4-1061·6) per 100 000 in 1990 to 677·3 (634·3-731·6) in 2023, with reductions of 36·5% in non-communicable diseases (NCDs) from 836·5 (808·4-861·7) in 1990 to 530·8 (488·4-580·8), 64·6% in communicable, maternal, neonatal, and nutritional diseases from 151·5 (135·5-167·0) in 1990 to 53·7 (43·5-63·9), but an increase of 77·5% in injuries from 52·3 (41·1-64·8) in 1990 to 92·8 (85·8-100·8) in 2023 due to the earthquakes. The top three causes of mortality in 2023 were ischaemic heart disease with an age-standardised mortality rate of 123·7 per 100 000 (95% UI 99·7-150·5), exposure to forces of nature (the February 2023 earthquakes) 65·2 (59·3-71·6), and stroke 57·0 (43·4-71·4). The leading age-standardised risk factors contributing to deaths in 2023 were high blood pressure with a rate of 137·4 per 100 000 (104·0-173·9), high BMI (86·9 [45·3-125·6]), and high fasting plasma glucose (85·8 [74·0-100·6]). Although our findings show a reduction in smoking-attributable burden, smoking remains the leading DALYs age-standardised risk factor for men in 2023 at 3928 per 100 000 (3098-4669). Among women, high BMI emerged as the leading risk factor of age-standardised DALYs at 2548 per 100 000 (1141-3719). Diabetes rose to become the third leading cause of health loss in 2023, and metabolic risks (ie, high BMI, high blood pressure, and high fasting plasma glucose) were the three leading risk factors for DALYs in 2023.
INTERPRETATION: Türkiye has achieved sustained health gains but faces rising NCDs, dietary, and behavioural risks that need to be monitored and addressed through multisectoral efforts. Strengthening prevention and early detection while leveraging digital health infrastructure is essential for Türkiye to build a strong health system.
FUNDING: Gates Foundation.

articles.title: Acute kidney injury and death in severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria: An individual patient data meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Serum or plasma concentrations of creatinine and urea are the usual laboratory parameters measured to assess acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with suspected severe malaria. Creatinine is preferred for estimation of the glomerular filtration rate, but the current threshold for defining severe malaria (>265 μmol/L or a urea >20 mmol/L) is based on adult values and does not reflect the large difference between children and adults in normal values resulting from differences in muscle mass. We reevaluated these thresholds and their prognostic significance in severe malaria using individual patient data from large prospective studies.
METHODS AND FINDINGS: We pooled individual patient data from 22,663 patients recruited into 14 studies of severe malaria of whom 16,441 were included in the primary analysis population. Patients were included in the primary analysis population if their age (if missing, imputed from weight or height), coma status on admission, and either an admission serum or plasma creatinine or urea measurement (blood urea nitrogen, BUN), were all recorded. The primary outcome was mortality by day 28. The secondary outcome was the admission plasma Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP2) concentration (a measure of parasite biomass). Bayesian penalised spline regression models were used to characterise the age-specific relationships (interaction with age) between the outcome and the absolute creatinine, the creatinine fold change relative to the age/weight predicted baseline, and the absolute urea. The models adjusted for coma status and calendar year, with nested random additive effects by study site and study. We estimated threshold plasma or serum creatinine and urea concentrations associated with >5% mortality with probability > 0.9. The majority (84%; 13,793/16,441) were children under 15 years of age. Current thresholds for AKI were associated with mortalities greater than 5%. An admission creatinine greater than three times the age/weight predicted baseline value was associated with >5% mortality. An admission urea >10 mmol/L had approximately similar prognostic value. A urea >10 mmol/L was 3.5 times more common in adults than children. In children <15 years of age, urea was a better prognostic indicator of death than creatinine and, unlike creatinine, correlated with the plasma PfHRP2 concentration. The main limitations of this analysis are the lack of metadata documenting laboratory methods and wide heterogeneity in eligibility criteria, such as creatinine or urea admission values for inclusion.
CONCLUSIONS: Admission serum or plasma creatinine >3 times the age/weight predicted baseline value (KDIGO AKI stage 3) can be used to define severe malaria AKI. In children, urea is a better predictor of the true infection biomass and a better prognostic indicator for death. We recommend the following as defining criteria for severe malaria: either a urea (BUN) threshold of 10 mmol/L for both children and adults, or simple age-based thresholds representing approximately >3 times fold change in creatinine from predicted baseline. These updated thresholds identify between 4 and 8 times more children with severe malaria AKI who are at a high risk of death.

articles.title: Peanut Allergy in Asian Children: From Regional Epidemiology and Molecular Sensitization to Oral Immunotherapy and Biologics.
articles.abstract: Peanut allergy has traditionally been considered less prevalent in Asia than in Western countries, where it is a major cause of food-induced anaphylaxis. Contemporary evidence challenges a uniform low-prevalence model and demonstrates marked geographic and methodological heterogeneity. Repeated surveys from Korea, Hong Kong, and Taiwan show increasing peanut-related clinical signals, Singapore confirms clinically relevant peanut allergy in early childhood, and Japanese hospitalization data identify peanut as an important cause of anaphylaxis among older children and adolescents. In contrast, India and parts of mainland China show low clinical burden or discordance between sensitization and overt allergy, while data remain sparse for several other Asian settings. These contrasts motivate investigation of genetic susceptibility, skin-barrier dysfunction, urbanization, dietary patterns, food processing, microbial exposures, and timing of oral allergen introduction. Evidence from LEAP has transformed prevention, whereas observational Asian cohorts have reported low allergy rates despite delayed introduction; these designs address different questions and do not establish equivalent preventive effects. Component-resolved diagnostics, particularly Ara h 2-specific IgE, can improve diagnostic assessment, although Asian thresholds remain supported mainly by single-center Korean and Singaporean studies without regional cross-validation. Peanut oral immunotherapy can increase reaction thresholds, but Asian evidence remains limited to small specialist cohorts, while epicutaneous immunotherapy and omalizumab provide additional evidence internationally. Future priorities include standardized surveillance, OFC-confirmed longitudinal Asian cohorts, locally validated diagnostic algorithms, culturally adapted prevention studies, pragmatic immunotherapy trials, and equitable access to adrenaline and specialist allergy care.

articles.title: Pyrroloquinoline Quinone as a Candidate Vitamin-like Accessory Factor: Evidence Gaps and Research Priorities.
articles.abstract: Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ), a bacterially derived ortho-quinone present in plant-based and fermented foods and in human milk, is proposed as a vitamin-like accessory factor. In this Perspective, we evaluate that proposal against the criteria historically used to establish nutritional essentiality. The evidence converges at several levels. PQQ-dependent pathways are conserved from bacteria to mammals. PQQ elicits growth, reproductive, and metabolic responses in invertebrates, fish, birds, rodents, and nonhuman primates. In mice and rats fed chemically defined diets, PQQ deprivation produces a reproducible, repletion-responsive phenotype. This phenotype includes impaired reproduction and neonatal growth, reduced immune responsiveness, lower energy expenditure with altered lipid metabolism, and diminished resilience to ischemic stress, with responses plateauing near 300 ng PQQ/g diet. Mechanistically, PQQ binds lactate dehydrogenase and shifts its kinetics toward pyruvate formation through redox cycling. It also acts as a selective agonist of the metabolite-sensing receptor GPR35 and engages the AMPK/SIRT1/PGC-1α, NRF-1, and KEAP1/NRF2 signaling pathways, which govern mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant defense. PQQ further intersects with folate, vitamin B-12, coenzyme Q10, and vitamin E metabolism. Small human trials report changes in inflammatory, mitochondrial-related, and cognitive endpoints, and preclinical toxicology indicates a wide safety margin. Nonetheless, PQQ does not yet meet the standard for an established human vitamin. No human deficiency syndrome has been described, validated status biomarkers and quantitative requirements are lacking, and food-composition data are incomplete. Dietary adducts such as imidazopyrroloquinoline are inconsistently measured, and the contribution of the gut microbiota is unresolved. We propose a research agenda comprising: 1) a standardized LC-MS/MS analysis of PQQ and its adducts, 2) biomarker validation, 3) human dose-response and depletion-repletion studies, 4) maternal-infant and older-adult cohorts, 5) mechanistic trials testing LDH and GPR35 engagement in human tissues, and 6) targeted efficacy trials in metabolic, reproductive, and age-related conditions. Statement of Significance: New and emerging evidence supporting the metabolic essentiality of PQQ is highlighted, including its roles as an enzyme redox accessory factor and as an agonist of receptors regulating mitochondrial functions. Recent studies across multiple species demonstrate the capacity of PQQ to modulate metabolism, with potential for life-stage-relevant health impacts, including early-life development, obesity-related conditions, and age-related functional decline. A framework is provided for future PQQ research.

articles.title: Sleep nudges: A scoping review of choice architecture interventions to address sleep health.
articles.abstract: Sleep-related problems affect 40-60% of adults globally, contributing to significant health and economic burdens. Choice architecture interventions, which structure decision environments to promote beneficial behaviors without restricting choice, have been studied in various health domains but remain relatively unexplored in the field of sleep. This scoping review mapped existing evidence on choice architecture interventions aimed at modifying sleep-related behaviors to improve sleep health outcomes, categorized interventions according to established taxonomies, and identified research gaps. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we systematically searched three databases, identifying six articles containing eight individual studies that met the inclusion criteria, reflecting the limited evidence available. Studies varied in design (predominantly randomized controlled trials), populations (children to adults), and intervention approaches. Most interventions combined multiple strategies, pairing information provision with micro-incentives (monetary or academic) or commitment facilitation. Primary outcomes focused on sleep duration, quality, and hygiene, assessed via actigraphy-based monitoring or self-report. Key gaps include limited population and technique diversity, multicomponent designs preventing component isolation, the assessment of individual sleep outcomes rather than sleep health from a multidimensional perspective, limited evaluation of the effects of these interventions on overall health, and minimal long-term follow-up.

articles.title: ERN EURO-NMD expert opinion on management of new biologic therapies in myasthenia gravis.
articles.abstract: Myasthenia Gravis is a potentially life-threatening autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction with fluctuating muscle weakness and fatigability. In recent years, the therapeutic landscape has been notably reshaped by the introduction of new therapies. These agents, primarily acting through complement inhibition or neonatal Fc-receptor blockade, have demonstrated significant efficacy and favorable safety profiles in randomized clinical trials and real-world settings. Their advent has refined clinical management, particularly in refractory patients, leading to meaningful improvements in patients' quality of life and future expectations. Meanwhile, in this evolving therapeutic landscape, new challenges and uncertainties in clinical decision-making have been raised, as new therapies are now part of the standard care in Myasthenia Gravis. Differences in regulatory agency approvals and reimbursement policies across Europe result in heterogeneous access to therapies, complicating treatment decisions and limiting shared real-world experiences. Consequently, clinicians face complex dilemmas regarding optimal patient selection, treatment choice, and long-term management strategies. To address these issues, a panel of experts, including adult and pediatric neurologists and patient representatives, within the framework of the European Reference Network for Neuromuscular Diseases convened to develop consensus-based positions. The aim of this work was to identify, explore, and discuss key challenges associated with the use of new therapies and to propose a practical approach to support clinicians in this rapidly evolving field. Given the variability in clinical approach, treatment availability and reimbursement policies across European healthcare systems, this position paper seeks to provide guidance that are adaptable across diverse settings. A literature review was conducted, focusing on pivotal clinical trials and real-world evidence. Eleven key topics were identified and discussed, and for each, consensus statements were developed and refined through a modified Delphi process: patient assessment from both clinician and patient perspectives; the role of autoantibodies and optimization of serological testing; selection of immunotherapies; definitions of treatment response and failure in the context of new therapies; strategies for switching between therapies; predictors of treatment response; management of concomitant therapies, including corticosteroids and conventional immunosuppressant; discontinuation strategies; their potential role as early-line therapies; their applicability in ocular MG; and future therapeutic perspectives, including ongoing clinical trials. In conclusion, new therapies represent a major advance in Myasthenia Gravis care but also introduce significant complexity. This expert position paper provides a framework to support clinicians in decision-making and highlights the need for harmonized guidelines and further research to optimize their use in routine practice.

articles.title: Treated and untreated maternal asthma and early pregnancy outcomes: a retrospective cohort study of 324,238 infants.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Continued use of asthma medication during pregnancy is recommended, because asthma exacerbations often increase during pregnancy, and poor control may adversely affect maternal and foetal health. However, evidence on whether adverse outcomes arise from the treatment itself or just the underlying disease remains inconsistent. This study examined the relationship between maternal asthma, and its medication, and early pregnancy outcomes.
METHODS: A retrospective birth cohort was constructed using population-wide linked Welsh health records of 324,238 infants born between 2009 and 2022. Logistic regression was used to investigate associations between maternal asthma (treated, untreated, and medication exposure) and pregnancy outcomes: stillbirth, iatrogenic and spontaneous preterm delivery, small/very small for gestational age (SGA/VSGA), and low Apgar score.
RESULTS: Of the 324,238 infants, 39,040 (12.0%) had mothers with asthma: 20,840 (6.4%) had treated asthma, 8,230 (2.5%) had untreated asthma, and 9,970 (3.1%) were prescribed asthma medications without recorded asthma diagnoses. Compared to offspring of mothers with no maternal asthma (reference group), those whose mothers had treated asthma had higher odds of SGA (aOR 1.13, 95% CI 1.07-1.19), VSGA (aOR 1.14, 95% CI 1.03-1.26), Apgar score < 7 (aOR 1.14, 95% CI 1.01-1.29), and iatrogenic preterm delivery (aOR 1.13, 95% CI 1.01-1.26). Associations were observed across multiple classes of asthma medication with stronger associations among the offspring of mothers prescribed more than one medication class and those with add-on therapies including long-acting muscarinic antagonists, short-acting muscarinic antagonists, leukotrienes antagonist and theophylline, consistent with more severe, or poorly controlled, asthma rather than medication effects. Untreated asthma was associated with higher risk of iatrogenic preterm delivery, and treated asthma was associated with lower risk of spontaneous preterm delivery (aOR 0.81, 95% CI 0.73-0.89). No associations were observed with stillbirth.
CONCLUSIONS: The non-specific associations observed across different classes of asthma medication and dose-relationships with polytherapy suggested confounding by indication and severity. The findings for iatrogenic preterm delivery further supported an effect of the underlying disease rather than its treatment. These findings, together with the lower risk of spontaneous preterm delivery among treated mothers, support guideline recommendations to continue asthma treatment during pregnancy.

articles.title: Associations between adverse childhood experiences and later-life multiple functional limitation in older adults across four cohorts.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The aim of this study is to evaluate the association between Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) and multiple functional limitation in older adults across various international settings.
METHODS: We used longitudinal data from 78,417 adults aged 50 years or older in four ageing cohorts: the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), and the Health and Retirement Study (HRS). Six ACE indicators were assessed retrospectively (physical abuse, emotional neglect, parental death, foster care placement, financial hardship, and parental unemployment) and analyzed in two ways: as the cumulative number of ACEs (categorized as 0, 1, 2, or ≥ 3), and as four ACE types (physical abuse, emotional neglect, adverse family environment, and economic adversity). At each survey wave, multiple functional limitation was measured as the number of impairments across six domains (hearing, vision, physical functioning, mobility, mental health, and cognition), giving a score from 0 to 6. Within each cohort, we used survey-weighted generalized estimating equations with a Poisson distribution to estimate associations with functional limitation, adjusting for age, sex, and survey wave. Cohort-specific risk ratios (RRs) were then combined using random-effects meta-analysis.
RESULTS: Across all cohorts, the proportion reporting at least one ACE ranged from 32.6% in ELSA to 66.9% in CHARLS. Compared with those reporting no ACE, the RRs (95% CI) for functional limitations were 1.17 (1.09-1.26) for one ACE, 1.29 (1.17-1.43) for two ACEs, and 1.39 (1.20-1.61) for three or more ACEs. Among the four ACE types, physical abuse (RR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.08-1.29), economic adversity (RR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.10-1.23), and emotional neglect (RR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.02-1.20) were each associated with higher functional limitation. Increased risks were observed across all six domains, with the strongest associations for mental disorders among individuals with three or more ACEs (RR, 1.82). The findings were consistent across cohorts and robust in sensitivity analyses.
CONCLUSIONS: ACEs were consistently associated with a greater risk of experiencing multiple functional limitations in later life, emphasizing the importance of mitigating childhood adversity to promote healthier ageing.

articles.title: Financial Incentives and Inequalities in Dental Care Delivery.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Patients with no prior relationship with a National Health Service (NHS) general dental practice in primary care are less likely to successfully obtain a dental appointment compared with returning patients. As part of a post-COVID-19 pandemic NHS Dental Recovery Plan, a new patient premium (NPP) scheme was introduced in England from March 1, 2024, to encourage dental practices to treat patients who had not seen an NHS dentist in the past 2 years.
OBJECTIVE: To assess whether the NPP scheme was associated with an increase in dental care utilization under the NHS.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This pooled cross-sectional study analyzed a national panel dataset of monthly dental activity data between March 2023 and March 2025 in England, using an interrupted time series approach with segmented regression analysis. All primary care practices that submitted claims for general dental services under the NHS were included.
EXPOSURE: Implementation of the NPP.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Number of new dental patients, total number of dental patients, and units of dental activity delivered.
RESULTS: A total of 4 377 699 new patients were seen under the NPP scheme; the mean (SD) count of adult patients was 235 380 (41 394) per month preintervention and 205 235 (18 950) postintervention, and of children was 140 502 (19 379) per month preintervention and 131 511 (14 752) per month postintervention. At the aggregate national level in England, there was no significant association between the NPP and the total number of new NHS dental patients. There was a monthly decline in new patients prior to (β, -76; 95% CI, -118 to -34) and at the point of (β, -665; 95% CI, -928 to -402) introduction of the NPP. There was a positive trend change after the NPP was implemented (β, 117; 95% CI, 58 to 175), driven primarily by an increase in the number of new adult patients and patients requiring band 2 and 3 treatments. Post-NPP trends varied across integrated care boards (ICBs). In ICBs where there was an increase in the number of new patients post-NPP, the total number of patients and dental activity delivered remained relatively constant or declined over time.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cross-sectional study of all NHS dental practices in England, implementation of the NPP was associated with an increase in the number of underserved new patients, but results varied by geographical area. Findings suggested a potential substitution effect whereby new patients displaced returning patients under the NHS in the absence of a corresponding increase in dental capacity.

articles.title: Gestational Weight Gain and Mortality Among Children in Brazil.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Gestational weight gain (GWG) is a key indicator of maternal nutritional status and has been associated with adverse perinatal outcomes. However, evidence of the association of GWG with child mortality remains limited, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the association between GWG and mortality among children younger than 5 years in Brazil.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This population-based cohort study used data from January 1, 2008, to December 31, 2020, from the 100 Million Brazilians Cohort, constructed through linkage of the Live Birth Information System, Food and Nutrition Surveillance System, and Mortality Information System databases, with statistical analyses performed between July and December 2025.
EXPOSURES: GWG was defined as the difference between third trimester and prepregnancy weight and classified as below, within, or above the 2009 US Institute of Medicine guidelines and Brazilian references for GWG.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcome was neonatal mortality, postneonatal mortality, infant mortality, and mortality among children younger than 5 years. Adjusted hazard ratios (AHRs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models controlling for maternal age, education, marital status, prenatal visits, prepregnancy body mass index (BMI), and year of birth. Analyses were stratified by prepregnancy BMI.
RESULTS: Among 792 935 singleton live births from 2008 to 2020 (51.1% boys; 683 656 [86.2%] born to mothers aged 20-34 years), 6105 deaths occurred among children younger than 5 years (0.8%). Compared with GWG within the guidelines, GWG below the guidelines was associated with higher risks of neonatal mortality (AHR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.11-1.32), postneonatal mortality (AHR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.04-1.28), infant mortality (AHR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.11-1.27), and mortality among children younger than 5 years (AHR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.12-1.26). Women with underweight had the greatest AHR for mortality among children younger than 5 years (1.47; 95% CI, 1.10-1.96). GWG above the guidelines was not consistently associated with mortality.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study, GWG below the guidelines was associated with increased early-life child mortality, particularly among women with underweight, highlighting the importance of monitoring maternal nutrition during pregnancy among vulnerable populations.

articles.title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus-Related Pediatric Intensive Care Unit Admissions in Children During Their Second RSV Season.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) hospitalization rates are highest among children younger than 2 years. For certain high-risk children entering their second RSV season, the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab is recommended. Little is known regarding preexisting health conditions as risk factors for RSV-related respiratory failure in children during their second RSV season.
OBJECTIVE: To describe children admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for severe RSV by classifying them by their nirsevimab eligibility status and preexisting health conditions, and comparing their demographic and clinical characteristics.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cohort study analyzed US children aged 8 to 23 months admitted to the PICU in 30 pediatric hospitals in the 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025 RSV seasons. All children had an RSV-positive result from a respiratory sample and received respiratory support with high-flow nasal cannula, noninvasive ventilation, or invasive mechanical ventilation. Analyses were based on the US criteria for second-season nirsevimab eligibility as recommended in August 2023.
EXPOSURE: Preexisting health conditions potentially associated with increased risk of severe RSV disease. Patients were classified into 4 mutually exclusive groups of eligibility status and preexisting health conditions: (1) met nirsevimab eligibility criteria, (2) with other identified RSV risk conditions (with some evidence of increased risk for severe RSV), (3) with other preexisting conditions, and (4) with no preexisting conditions.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Patient demographic characteristics and level of respiratory support received were compared by level of preexisting health conditions.
RESULTS: A total of 574 children (median [IQR] age, 1.2 [1.1-1.5] years; 317 males [55.2%]) were included. Overall, 47 patients (8.2%) met the nirsevimab eligibility criteria, 76 (13.2%) had other identified RSV risk conditions, 96 (16.7%) had other preexisting conditions, and 355 (61.8%) had no preexisting conditions. A higher proportion of children who met nirsevimab eligibility criteria required invasive mechanical ventilation vs children with other identified RSV risk conditions, those with other preexisting health conditions, or those with no preexisting health conditions (40.4% [19 of 47] vs 17.1% [13 of 76], 10.4% [10 of 96], 5.9% [21 of 355]; P for trend <.001).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among children admitted to the PICU for severe RSV, 8.2% met the nirsevimab eligibility criteria and 13.2% had other identified RSV risk conditions. These findings might help inform future deliberations regarding second RSV season recommendations for nirsevimab eligibility in the US.

articles.title: Milk Fat Globule Membrane-Enriched Formula and Cognition Among Formula-Fed Infants: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: The absence of milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) in infant formula may contribute to the differences between breastfed and formula-fed infants.
OBJECTIVE: To test whether MFGM-enriched infant formula benefits cognitive development of exclusively formula-fed infants.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This clinician-blinded, researcher-blinded, and participant-blinded randomized clinical trial of exclusively formula-fed infants with a reference group (exclusively breastfed) included full-term singleton infants under 2 months of age, who were recruited from the community (May 2020 to April 2022). Follow-up was completed in June 2024 and analyses completed in September 2025.
INTERVENTIONS: Randomized infants received either MFGM-enriched formula (treatment group: 0.55 g per 100.00 g of MFGM component phospholipid from MFGM Lipid 100 [New Zealand Milk Products, Fonterra Co-Operative Group Limited]) or standard formula (control group: no added MFGM, 0.29 g per 100.00 g of MFGM component phospholipid) from randomization to 12 months of age.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, 4th Edition scales for cognitive, language, motor, emotional, and behavioral development, in which the mean (SD) score is 100 (15), with scores below 85 classified as delayed, were administered at ages 12 months and 24 months; the primary outcome was the 12-month cognitive score. Caregivers reported health, language, development, growth, safety, and tolerance.
RESULTS: There were 416 randomized formula-fed infants (mean [SD] age, 36.6 [11.5] days; 209 males [50.2%]) and 204 reference group infants. Primary outcome data were available for 382 randomized infants (91.8%), including 193 (93.2%) of 207 in the treatment group and 189 (90.4%) of 209 in the control group. The mean (SD) 12-month cognitive scores in the treatment group (100.1 [11.9]) and control group (99.4 [14.1]) were not significant (adjusted mean difference, 0.68 [95% CI, -1.94 to 3.31]; P = .61). There was a significantly lower risk of delayed cognition (<85) at age 12 months in the treatment group compared with the control group (10.0 [4.8%] vs 24.1 [11.5%]; adjusted relative risk, 0.42 [95% CI, 0.20-0.90]; P = .03), and the mean (SD) language scores at age 24 months were higher in the treatment group compared with the control group (93.0 [16.3] vs 90.0 [16.6]; adjusted mean difference, 2.87 [95% CI, 0.10-5.65]; P = .04), although this difference was not statistically significant after controlling for caregiver educational level. Other secondary developmental outcomes, as well as growth and safety outcomes, were mostly not significant.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial of MFGM-supplemented formula compared with standard formula among nonbreastfed infants, mean cognitive scores were not improved, although a reduction in the number of infants with cognitive delay is worthy of further investigation.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier: ACTRN12620000552987.

articles.title: Bystander CPR Type and Outcomes After Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Compression-only cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CO-CPR) has been widely promoted to encourage bystander intervention in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but long-term trends in bystander CPR and the associations between CPR type and outcomes in pediatric OHCA remain unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate temporal trends in bystander CPR type and the associations with clinical outcomes among children with OHCA in Japan.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cohort study included patients aged 17 years or younger with known receipt of bystander CPR documented in the nationwide All-Japan Utstein Registry from January 1, 2005, to December 31, 2023. Data analysis was performed from November 24, 2025, to September 2, 2026, including additional analyses conducted during the revision process.
EXPOSURES: Bystander CPR was categorized as rescue-breathing CPR (RB-CPR), CO-CPR, or no bystander CPR.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate; secondary outcomes were 30-day survival rate and prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Temporal trends were assessed with multinomial logistic regression, and associations between CPR type and outcomes were evaluated using modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation, with CO-CPR serving as the reference.
RESULTS: Among 26 785 pediatric patients with OHCA (median [IQR] age, 2.0 [0-12] years; 16 254 males [60.7%]), 6543 (24.4%) received RB-CPR, 9112 (34.0%) received CO-CPR, and 11 130 (41.6%) received no bystander CPR. The adjusted probability of CO-CPR increased from 14.6% (95% CI, 13.1%-16.1%) in 2005 to 55.1% (95% CI, 52.5%-57.6%) in 2023, whereas RB-CPR declined from 41.7% (95% CI, 39.7%-43.7%) to 10.4% (95% CI, 8.7%-12.1%). The adjusted probability of receiving no bystander CPR plateaued at approximately 35.0% after 2013. Neurologically favorable 30-day survival rate occurred in 3.6% receiving no bystander CPR, 9.5% receiving CO-CPR, and 16.0% receiving RB-CPR. Compared with CO-CPR, RB-CPR was associated with a higher 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 1.71; 95% CI, 1.57-1.86), 30-day survival rate (ARR, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.42-1.61), and prehospital ROSC (ARR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.51-1.75), whereas receipt of no bystander CPR was associated with lower probabilities of these outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study of children with OHCA, increasing CO-CPR use coincided with declining RB-CPR but not with further reductions in untreated arrests after 2013. No bystander CPR was associated with worse outcomes compared with CO-CPR and RB-CPR. RB-CPR had more favorable outcomes than CO-CPR, supporting the continued importance of rescue breathing in pediatric resuscitation.

articles.title: Timing of Antenatal Care, Stillbirth, and Infant Mortality in Migrant Mothers in Australia.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Timely antenatal care (ANC) reduces pregnancy risks, yet the association between delayed ANC and stillbirth or infant mortality among migrant mothers in Australia has not previously been investigated.
OBJECTIVE: To examine whether delayed ANC is associated with higher stillbirth and infant mortality among Australia-born compared with migrant mothers.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective cohort study assessed births to non-Indigenous mothers in New South Wales from January 1, 2002, to December 31, 2020, followed up to infant age of 1 year. Mothers were categorized as Australia-born, migrant from English-speaking country (ESM), or migrant from non-English-speaking country (non-ESM). Data were analyzed between August 2025 and June 2026.
EXPOSURES: Timing of first ANC, defined as 12 weeks or earlier, 13 to 19 weeks, 20 weeks or later, or no ANC.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcome was stillbirth (at ≥20 weeks) and infant mortality (at prehospital discharge, posthospital discharge, or 1 year). Adjusted relative risks (ARRs) were estimated using Poisson regression models, stratified by migration group.
RESULTS: This study included 1 720 033 births (median [IQR] maternal age, 31.2 [27.4-34.8] years; 884 235 male infants [51.4%]), including 1 132 193 (65.8%) to Australia-born, 116 026 (6.7%) to ESM, and 471 814 (27.4%) to non-ESM mothers. Late ANC (>12 weeks) was more common in non-ESM mothers (190 338 [40.3%]) than Australia-born (334 790 [29.6%]) or ESM (41 029 [35.4%]) mothers. In cross-group comparisons, non-ESM mother status was associated with higher risk of adverse outcomes regardless of ANC timing. Compared with Australia-born mothers with early ANC (≤12 weeks), a higher risk of stillbirth (ARR, 1.25; 95% CI, 1.18-1.33) and 1-year (ARR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.22-1.44), predischarge (ARR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.25-1.54), and postdischarge (ARR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.03-1.37) infant mortality was observed in non-ESM mothers accessing ANC by 12 weeks. Similar risk patterns were observed in non-ESM mothers with late ANC. In within-group comparisons, among Australia-born mothers, each category of delayed ANC was associated with higher risk. No ANC was associated with the highest risks across all maternal groups for stillbirth and 1-year infant mortality. For non-ESM mothers, late ANC (≥20 weeks) was associated with a lower risk of predischarge mortality (ARR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.61-0.92) but a higher risk of postdischarge mortality (ARR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.02-1.65).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study of 1.72 million births, higher risks of stillbirths and infant mortalities were observed in non-ESM mothers regardless of ANC timing, warranting further investigation.

articles.title: Climate Vulnerability, Historical Redlining, and Children's Mental Health Care Use.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Structural inequities stemming from historical redlining and environmental injustice have created varying levels of risk among marginalized communities. However, the association of climate risk and structural racism with pediatric mental health care use remains underexplored.
OBJECTIVES: To examine associations between climate vulnerability and pediatric mental health care use, and to assess whether these associations vary by historical redlining status.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cross-sectional study of children aged younger than 18 years residing in New York State between 2017 and 2022 used all-payer hospital administrative data from the New York State Department of Health. Statistical analysis was conducted from January 2025 through February 2026.
MAIN OUTCOME AND MEASURES: Outcomes included mental health-related emergency department (ED) and outpatient visits identified using International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision-coded mental health diagnosis subtypes (eg, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), aggregated at the census-tract level. The primary exposure was climate-specific Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles (where 1 indicates low climate vulnerability and 4 indicates high climate vulnerability). Poisson regression models were conducted to examine associations between Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles and mental health-related health care utilization, including interactions with neighborhood-level redlining status (Home Owners' Loan Corporation grades C/D vs A/B) and subtype-specific analyses. Models adjusted for age, sex, self- or guardian-reported race and ethnicity, and neighborhood-level covariates, with coefficients reported as rate ratios (RRs).
RESULTS: A total of 553 134 mental health-related visits were included (mean [SD] age, 7.2 [5.8] years; 285 526 male [51.6%]). Compared with children living in areas with the lowest climate vulnerability, those living in the highest-vulnerability areas had higher outpatient visit rates (RR, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.72-2.27) and non-statistically significantly higher ED visit rates (RR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.96-1.35). Associations between high climate vulnerability and mental health-related health care utilization varied by redlining status. In historically redlined neighborhoods, high climate vulnerability was associated with outpatient health care utilization (RR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.44-1.51; P < .001 for interaction) and, to a lesser extent, ED utilization (RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.09; P < .001 for interaction); in nonredlined neighborhoods high climate vulnerability was associated with lower outpatient health care utilization (RR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.45-0.49; P < .001 for interaction) and not associated with ED utilization (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.93-1.07). Associations also varied across mental health diagnosis subtypes, with higher climate vulnerability associated with increased health care utilization for most diagnosis subtypes.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cross-sectional study of children, residence in historically redlined and climate-vulnerable neighborhoods was associated with higher rates of mental health-related health care utilization. These findings highlight geographic patterns in mental health-related health care utilization that may be relevant to future research on climate preparedness, mental health services, culturally responsive care, and access to services for children experiencing climate-related stressors and structural inequities.

articles.title: Localization mechanisms and function of postsynaptic Kv7 (KCNQ) channels and their reduction in KCNQ2 epileptic encephalopathy.
articles.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
articles.abstract: Kv7 channels composed of Kv7.2 and Kv7.3 subunits are enriched in neuronal axons where their hyperpolarizing potassium current suppresses repetitive and burst firing of action potentials. Mutations in their genes, KCNQ2 and KCNQ3, cause neonatal epilepsy, underscoring their critical role in regulating neuronal excitability. In this study, we provide evidence that Kv7 channels are present at and near the postsynaptic density within dendritic spines of hippocampal neurons, where their current decreases calcium influx through NMDA receptors. This spine localization is promoted by heteromerization of Kv7.2 and Kv7.3 and their binding to AnkyrinG-190, which is the only AnkyrinG isoform present in dendritic spines. Lastly, spine localization of Kv7 channels and their ability to suppress NMDA receptor activity are markedly reduced by select variants of KCNQ2 that cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). These findings reveal a subcellular population of Kv7 channels that can dampen excitatory synaptic transmission and implicate their dysregulation in KCNQ2-associated DEE.

articles.title: From broad suppression to precision targeting: the new era of antigen-specific immunotherapy for type 1 diabetes.
articles.abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the selective destruction of pancreatic β-cells driven by autoreactive immune responses. In recent decades, the global incidence of T1D has risen markedly, with the most rapid increase observed among children and adolescents, imposing a substantial burden on healthcare systems worldwide. Conventional treatment primarily relies on exogenous insulin administration, which manages hyperglycemia but does not address the underlying autoimmune pathology or restore endogenous insulin production. Antigen-specific immunotherapy (ASI) has emerged as a promising strategy that may restore antigen-specific immune tolerance via multiple mechanisms, including clonal deletion/ anergy, immune deviation, induction of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and type 1 regulatory T (Tr1) cells, and tolerogenic antigen presentation. ASI may help preserve residual β-cell function and potentially modify disease progression. This review comprehensively summarizes recent advances in ASI for T1D, with a focus on the biological features of key T1D autoantigens, optimization of antigen delivery strategies, and prospects for clinical translation.

articles.title: Identification of phenotypic abnormalities and effector function impairment in natural killer cells of patients with ataxia-telangiectasia.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) is a rare inherited disorder resulting from mutations in the ATM gene and characterized by progressive neurodegeneration, immunological abnormalities, and increased infection and cancer susceptibility. There is no cure for A-T, and life expectancy is drastically reduced because of pulmonary disease and cancer. Humoral or T/B-cell deficiency was associated with reduced survival in A-T patients, although the findings remain controversial. Conversely, A-T patients display normal numbers of NK cells, crucial components of the antitumor and antiviral innate immunity. The goal of the present study was to investigate the function of NK cells in A-T.
METHODS: Peripheral blood NK cells of 31 A-T patients were analyzed via flow cytometry to assess their distribution across subpopulations and expression of maturation markers, receptors and effector molecules. Additionally, we assessed the capacity of NK cells to kill K562 cells and to produce IFN-γ in response to IL-12/IL-15/IL-18 stimulation. The plasma levels of soluble ligands for the NKG2D receptor (sNKG2DLs) and cytokines were measured via ELISA.
RESULTS: Compared with control NK cells, A-T patient NK cells presented higher frequencies of the CD56bright and CD56dimCD16- subsets and contraction of the highly cytotoxic CD56dim subset that, however, showed a normal maturation pattern. The expression of the main activating/inhibitory receptors was conserved on A-T NK cells, except for the up- and downregulation of PD-1 and NKG2D, respectively. NKG2D downregulation correlated with accumulation of the sNKG2DLs sMICA and sULBP2 in patient plasma. Importantly, A-T NK cells were inefficient at producing IFN-γ upon stimulation and strongly impaired at killing tumor targets, dysfunctions that were reproduced by inhibiting ATM in PBMCs of healthy individuals. Finally, in A-T plasma, we detected elevated levels of IL-6, which correlated with NK-cell phenotypic alterations and reduced IFN-γ response, and increased levels of TGF-β, which correlated with impaired NK-cell cytotoxicity.
